newsitem.title: USA: US strike issues may boost wage worries-Challenger.
newsitem.headline: US strike issues may boost wage worries-Challenger.

text.p: The United Parcel Service strike may be over, but workplace issues at the forefront of the dispute could lead to a rise in inflation despite a strong economy, according to Challenger, Gray & Christmas, Inc.

"I think (the recent UPS strike) has real potential to be the signal event that creates the wage inflation, the absence of which has mystified economists for the last two years," said John Challenger, executive vice president of the international outplacement consulting firm.
Local leaders of the Teamsters Union will meet in Washington later Tuesday to vote on a tentative settlement agreement with UPS, a union spokesman said.
Pending ratification of the deal, U.S. Labor Secretary Alexis Herman said workers should be back on the job by mid-week, thereby ending a 15-day walkout.
Challenger said it was not only part-time or hourly workers who have been affected by the UPS strike.
"Wage stagnation has been felt by all employees. Since 1989, corporate profits have soared 18 percent, while wages are up just 2.8 percent," he said.
The Labor Department reported earlier this month that average hourly earnings held steady at $12.23 an hour in July. That compares with earnings of $11.81 an hour in July of 1996.

Meanwhile, inflation at the retail level as measured by the Consumer Price Index rose just 0.2 percent last month, bringing the rate for the first seven months of the year to 2.2 percent, compared with 1996.
Challenger said inflationary wage pressures could lead to a rise in interest rates to counteract ensuing inflation.
However, he added that he did not foresee any policy change at Tuesday's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting in Washington.

Federal Reserve Board Chairman Alan Greenspan had been "closely watching the mood of the workplace, reportedly asking to see terms of UPS settlement proposals, trying to gauge if and when employees might push for higher wages, creating a need for higher price tags on goods and services," he said.
Indeed, in a Reuters survey, 31 economists unanimously agreed that the Fed was unlikely to raise short-term interest rates due to healthy economic growth and no major concerns about inflation.
The FOMC is expected to announce its decision on interest rates Tuesday at about 1415 EDT/1815 GMT.
